name: Three-Column Cash Book

origin.note: A cash-book layout commonly records cash, bank and discount columns; local teaching and presentation can vary.

theory.definition: A cash book records cash and bank receipts and payments; a three-column form includes discount columns.
theory.purpose: It combines a chronological cash record with cash and bank ledger information.
principles: Receipts and payments are recorded on opposite sides.
Cash and bank balances are tracked separately.
Discount entries require the related transaction context.
rules: Enter receipts on the debit side and payments on the credit side.
Record contra transfers on both cash and bank sides where applicable.
Reconcile book bank balance with bank evidence.

posting_steps: Enter amount in cash or bank column.
Record discount in its appropriate column when applicable.
Mark transfers between cash and bank as contra entries.
Balance and reconcile the bank column.
common_errors: Omitting one side of a contra transfer.
Confusing discount allowed and discount received.
Failing to reconcile the bank column.

exercise.prompt: Record a cash receipt, bank payment and cash-to-bank transfer.
exercise.answer_rule: Record each transaction on the correct side and ensure any contra transfer appears on both cash and bank columns.

on_statements: Cash and bank balances contribute to the statement of financial position and cash flow information.
on_decisions: Monitor available cash and bank balances.
Review cash movement and prepare bank reconciliation.
risk_if_wrong: Cash errors can distort liquidity information and conceal missing receipts or payments.

depth.level_1: A cash record with cash, bank and discount columns.
depth.level_2: Record receipts and payments on opposite sides, handle contra transfers, and reconcile bank activity.
depth.level_3: Column conventions and discount treatment vary in teaching contexts; compare the cash book with a journal and a bank reconciliation.

needs_verification: Confirm local column order and discount posting conventions for the intended jurisdiction.
